title: Review: Cardiovascular disease and risk; The heart and cardiac cycle; Control of heart rate and ECGs; Blood clotting and blood cells
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EX13a#t1 term and clue written for the game; EX08#t2 term and clue written for the game; IM10#t2 term and clue written for the game; IM10#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX07#N.3, EX08#N.7, EX13a#N.5, IM10#N.7, EX07#N.6, EX13a#N.11a, IM10#N.11b, EX07#N.14, IM10#N.3, IM10#N.5. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Coronary arteries
items.clue: Vessels branching from the aorta that supply heart muscle with oxygen and glucose.

items.label: Sinoatrial node
items.clue: The pacemaker: sends out a wave of electrical excitation that starts each heartbeat

items.label: Thrombin
items.clue: Enzyme produced by a cascade of reactions; it acts on a soluble substance in the blood.

items.label: Platelets
items.clue: Stick to a damaged vessel and to each other, forming a plug, and release clotting factors.

questions.stem: The wall of the left ventricle is about three times thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. Which statement correctly explains this difference?

options.text: The left ventricle pumps a larger volume of blood at each beat than the right ventricle, so it needs more muscle.
The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, which offer more resistance to flow than the rest of the body does.
The left ventricle must generate a much higher pressure to drive blood through the whole systemic circulation.
The left ventricle gets a stronger nerve impulse from the brain at each beat, so it has built up more muscle.

questions.stem: On an ECG recorded at 25 mm s⁻¹, the distance between two R peaks is 30 mm. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
questions.explanation: R–R time = 30 ÷ 25 = 1.2 s. Rate = 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50 beats min⁻¹.

questions.stem: A blood clot completely occludes a branch of a coronary artery. What is the direct consequence?

options.text: Blood can no longer pass through the chambers of the heart, so the heart stops beating almost at once.
The region of cardiac muscle supplied by that branch is deprived of oxygen and its cells die.
Fat from the diet keeps building up on the surface of the clot until the artery bursts open.
The muscle in the artery wall contracts to force the clot along, tearing the artery wall.

questions.explanation: The coronary arteries supply the cardiac muscle of the heart wall. Occlusion cuts off the oxygen supply to the muscle beyond the block, so the cells there die: a myocardial infarction. The damaged region may then fail to contract properly.

questions.stem: The drug warfarin blocks the use of vitamin K in the liver. The liver needs vitamin K to make prothrombin. What happens to the blood of a person taking warfarin?

options.text: It clots more slowly, because without vitamin K platelets cannot stick to form a plug.
It clots normally, because platelets alone form the clot that seals a cut.
It clots normally, because fibrin threads are already present in the plasma.
It clots more slowly, because less prothrombin means less thrombin is made.

questions.explanation: Less thrombin converts less fibrinogen to fibrin, so the mesh forms more slowly. Warfarin is used to prevent unwanted clots.

questions.stem: The sinoatrial node fires. Which sequence of events then follows in the left side of the heart?

options.text: The atrium and the ventricle contract at the same moment, and the atrioventricular and semilunar valves open together to let blood into the aorta.
The atrium contracts, filling the ventricle; the ventricle then contracts, shutting the atrioventricular valve and opening the semilunar valve; then both relax.
Muscles attached to the valves pull them open one after the other, and the ventricle contracts only after both valves have been opened.
A nerve impulse from the brain reaches the ventricle first, so the ventricle contracts and then the atrium contracts to refill it.

questions.explanation: Atrial systole completes ventricular filling. The ventricle's rising pressure shuts the AV valve and, once above aortic pressure, opens the semilunar valve. Diastole follows.

questions.stem: A man has atheroma in a carotid artery, which carries blood to the brain. A plaque ruptures. What is most likely to happen next?

options.text: Fat from his blood keeps sticking to the exposed plaque until, over a few hours, the carotid artery bursts open.
The ruptured plaque stops blood passing through the chambers of his heart, so no blood reaches his brain.
The smooth muscle of the artery wall contracts to push the broken plaque along the vessel to his brain.
A clot forms at the rupture and blocks this artery or a smaller one; brain tissue beyond lacks oxygen.

questions.explanation: Same chain as a heart attack: damaged wall → plaque → rupture → clot → occlusion. In the brain, the result is a stroke.

questions.stem: In a stained blood film, a cell is larger than a red blood cell. Its nucleus has three lobes, and its cytoplasm is granular. Which cell is it, and what does it do?

options.text: A lymphocyte, which makes antibodies.
A monocyte, which becomes a macrophage.
A polymorph, which engulfs pathogens.
A platelet, which starts clotting.

questions.explanation: A lobed nucleus and granular cytoplasm identify a polymorph, a phagocyte.

questions.stem: Pressures in the right side of a heart, early in ventricular systole: right atrium 0.4 kPa; right ventricle 1.0 kPa and rising; pulmonary artery 1.3 kPa. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The atrioventricular valve is open, because pressure in the ventricle is higher than in the atrium.
The semilunar valve is open, because the ventricle is contracting.
Both valves will open when the pacemaker sends a nerve signal to them.
Both valves are shut; the semilunar valve will open once ventricular pressure exceeds 1.3 kPa.

questions.explanation: Ventricle above atrium shuts the AV valve; ventricle below artery keeps the semilunar valve shut. As pressure keeps rising, it opens.

questions.stem: Fibrinogen circulates in the blood all the time. Why does a clot form at a cut, but not throughout the blood vessels?

options.text: Thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin, is made only where clotting factors are released.
Fibrinogen turns into fibrin only when the blood at a cut is exposed to the air.
Fibrin threads are in the blood all the time, but they tangle together only where blood flow slows at a cut.
Platelets stick together into a plug at the cut, and this plug alone is the clot, with no plasma proteins needed.

questions.explanation: The cascade starts only at the wound, so thrombin, and so fibrin, forms only there. Elsewhere fibrinogen stays soluble.

questions.stem: Fibrinogen circulates in the plasma of healthy people all the time, yet clots form only where a blood vessel has been damaged. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin only when it is exposed to the air at an open wound, so a clot cannot form inside a vessel that is intact.
Fibrin is already present in the plasma, but its threads only become tangled into a mesh where the flow of blood is disturbed by damage.
The cascade has so many steps that it is too slow to finish unless the blood is held still against the wall of a damaged vessel.
Thrombin, the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, is produced by a cascade that starts only when platelets release clotting factors at a site of damage.
